title: Husky Robotics — Hand Board
summary: Wrote bare-metal C on STM32G4 to control a robotic hand — stepper motors, solenoids, lasers, and a custom FDCAN communication stack with real-time fault recovery.
details:
The hand board is the brain of the robotic end-effector on Husky Robotics’ rover. The goal: give the rover a hand that can grip, actuate, and sense — reliably, over a noisy CAN bus, in the middle of a competition.

How it all works together:
The STM32G4 sits at the center, coordinating stepper motors (via DRV8825 drivers), solenoids, linear actuators, and a laser — all running concurrently. Each subsystem talks to the MCU over GPIO, PWM, or SPI, while the board itself communicates upstream to the rover’s main computer over FDCAN.

Challenges:
• Motor noise coupling into signal lines caused phantom GPIO triggers during high-current stepper steps. Fixed by adding snubber logic in firmware and tightening PCB ground planes.
• FDCAN synchronization was tricky — getting heartbeat timing right so the E-STOP would trigger fast enough under fault but not false-fire during normal latency spikes took a lot of oscilloscope time.
• The DRV8825 has no built-in position feedback — so I built a real-time step counter with interrupt-driven limit switch callbacks to give the system axis homing and bounds checking.
• Laser PWM flicker at low duty cycles was visible and unacceptable. Switching from 8-bit to 10-bit TIM2 resolution fixed it — but required recalculating all prescaler values and retesting the full intensity range.
• Coordinating solenoids, steppers, and actuators in a single control loop without blocking — everything had to be non-blocking so FDCAN messages were never missed.

What I learned:
Writing bare-metal firmware forces you to understand the hardware completely. There’s no RTOS scheduler to hide behind — if your timing is off by a few microseconds, the motor stutters or the E-STOP misfires. It taught me to think in terms of hardware states, not just software logic.
tech: C, STM32G474, FDCAN, PWM, DRV8825, Stepper Motors

title: GPS-Navigating Mecanum Rover
summary: Built an autonomous holonomic rover on RP2040 — custom UART/I2C drivers for GPS and IMU, mecanum kinematics for four-motor control, and HIL test infrastructure.
details:
This project started as a question: could a rover navigate to a GPS waypoint on its own, with a MCU cheap enough to hand to a whole club of students? I built it around an RP2040, writing everything in bare-metal C from the ground up — no off-the-shelf robotics stack to lean on.

The rover reads its position from a NEO-6M GPS module and its orientation from a BNO055 IMU, both over custom UART and I2C drivers I wrote myself since nothing off-the-shelf fit the timing I needed. Getting those two sensors talking cleanly to the RP2040 took a fair amount of trial and error — GPS fixes come in slow and noisy, so the firmware has to fuse that with the IMU's faster, drift-prone heading data to get something the drive loop can actually trust.

Drive itself is mecanum — four wheels, each independently PWM-controlled, which means the rover can strafe sideways or spin in place instead of just turning like a car. I worked out the kinematic equations by hand so I actually understood why a given wheel-speed combination produced a given motion, rather than copying a formula I didn't trust.

Before I ever let it loose outdoors, I built out hardware-in-the-loop test infrastructure so I could validate the controller against simulated sensor input first — cheaper than crashing a real rover into a wall to find a bug. Once it worked, the whole thing became a teaching platform: I documented the flashing and validation process well enough that a 30-member club could pick it up and build on it themselves.
tech: C, RP2040, UART, I2C, NEO-6M GPS, BNO055 IMU

title: Vaakya — Wearable Real-Time Captioning
summary: AI glasses for real-time captioning on Raspberry Pi — zero-persistence, fully offline audio pipeline, sub-second captions at 60 FPS. Selected for the Lavin x Anthropic entrepreneurship program.
details:
Vaakya is a pair of AI glasses I engineered for real-time captioning, built around a zero-persistence, fully offline audio pipeline on a Raspberry Pi. The design principle was privacy-first from the start: for a high-stakes communication setting — a doctor's office, a private conversation — nothing about what's said should ever leave the device or get written to disk.

Getting captions out fast enough to feel real-time was the core engineering problem. A single pipeline that captures audio and then runs inference in sequence is too slow on a Raspberry Pi, so I optimized a dual-threaded inference pipeline where capture and inference run concurrently, which is what makes sub-second captions possible at all. Those captions get pushed to a Vufine head-mounted display at 60 FPS, so the text keeps pace with a live conversation instead of visibly lagging behind it.

The project was selected for the Lavin x Anthropic entrepreneurship program, and I was awarded $2,000 in funding from UW's Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship after pitching it to industry professionals and investors.
tech: Python, Vosk STT, Raspberry Pi, Docker

title: Embassy — STM32 HAL Fixes
summary: Diagnosed and fixed a flash erase bug and a related bounds-check bug on chips with non-contiguous flash banks, and root-caused an I2C slave NVIC interrupt hang from a community bug report.
details:
I contribute to embassy-rs, the async embedded framework a lot of the Rust embedded community builds on, and three bugs I chased down there turned into merged fixes.

The first was a flash erase bug on the STM32G473CB caused by non-contiguous flash banks — the chip has a physical gap between Bank1 and Bank2 that the erase logic didn't account for. I fixed it by correcting the bank-relative page indexing, and added an async bank-mode sanity check so the driver fails early if the configured bank mode doesn't match the chip's actual option bytes, instead of silently misbehaving.

While I was in there I found a related bug: the flash bounds check was rejecting valid Bank2 addresses on the same non-contiguous-bank chips, because it validated offsets against total flash size instead of the chip's true addressable span. I fixed that by bounding offsets against the real address range.

The third came from a community bug report describing an I2C slave interrupt hang. I traced it back to an unbound interrupt handler that new_blocking() was leaving enabled — since blocking mode never registers a handler, a real interrupt firing had nowhere to go and the slave hung. I fixed the masking logic so blocking mode no longer enables interrupts it doesn't use, and closed a separate ADDRIE race condition against the interrupt handler while root-causing it.

title: Microsoft CFU Protocol — Rust Firmware
summary: Identified and fixed a code-duplication risk in Microsoft's open-source CFU firmware service, simplifying response logic shared between the Buffer and Splitter components.
details:
I contributed to the Open Device Partnership, a Microsoft-affiliated open-source project, working in production Rust firmware on the Component Firmware Update (CFU) protocol — the service responsible for getting firmware updates safely onto a device.

While reading through the CFU service, I identified a code-duplication risk: the Buffer and Splitter components each maintained their own independent copy of the validation logic for invalid version and content rejection. Two independent copies of the same logic is exactly the kind of thing that quietly drifts out of sync over time — a fix applied to one copy with no reason to touch the other. I simplified the response logic by moving that common code into a shared module used by both components, so there's one implementation instead of two that are supposed to agree.

title: Electric Skateboard
summary: Built a dual-motor electric skateboard with brushless DC hub motors and a VESC motor controller, powered by a custom 10S3P lithium-ion battery pack (36V, 7.8Ah).
details:
This one started as a personal project back in 2023 and I've kept coming back to it since. I built a dual-motor electric skateboard from the ground up — brushless DC hub motors for drive, and a VESC (Vedder Electronic Speed Controller) handling the motor control side, which is the same open-source controller a lot of the DIY e-skate community builds around.

The part I spent the most time getting right was the battery: a custom 10S3P lithium-ion pack — 10 cells in series for a 36V nominal pack voltage, 3 in parallel per group for capacity, landing at 7.8Ah total. Building a pack by hand means owning every part of that decision: cell selection, spot-welding the nickel strips, balancing taps for the BMS, and making sure the whole thing can deliver the current two hub motors actually pull under load without sagging or overheating. It's a good reminder that battery systems aren't just a spec on a datasheet — they're a physical thing you have to build correctly or it becomes a safety problem, not just a performance one.
